Square-root logarithmic bounds for the arithmetic complexity of factorial multiplesThanks: Corresponding author: Liang Zhang.

Liang Zhang Email address: tensor@pku.edu.cn
Abstract.

Assume that the Riemann zeta function has no zeros in ℜ⁡(s)>1−δ\Re(s)>1-\delta, s≠1s\neq 1, for some fixed 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2. We prove that, for every sufficiently large integer kk, a positive multiple mk​k!m_{k}k! has arithmetic complexity τ⁡(mk​k!)≤exp⁡(C​log⁡k​log⁡log​k)\tau(m_{k}k!)\leq\exp(C\sqrt{\log k\log\log k}), where CC depends only on δ\delta. We first establish a smooth-number asymptotic at every sufficiently large center xx in intervals of length at least x3/4x^{3/4}. Combining this estimate with an established genus-two construction yields the arithmetic bound without Cheng’s conjecture on smooth numbers in elliptic Hasse intervals. The bound includes the cost of constructing all integer parameters. This work was carried out with assistance from the UniMath model, developed by UniDT (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra.

Key words and phrases: 
arithmetic complexity, factorial multiples, smooth numbers, short intervals, genus-two Jacobians
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11Y55; Secondary 11N25, 11G20, 68Q15

1. Introduction

The purpose of this paper is to bound the arithmetic complexity of a suitable positive multiple of each factorial. The main result, Theorem A, obtains the scale exp⁡(Oδ​(log⁡k​log⁡log​k))\exp(O_{\delta}(\sqrt{\log k\log\log k})) from a fixed zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function, without assuming Cheng’s smooth-number conjecture for elliptic Hasse intervals. Here τ⁡(n)\tau(n) measures the number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct nn from 11 and 22, and μ⁡(k)\mu(k) denotes the least such cost among positive multiples of k!k!. The precise circuit model and both quantities are specified in Definition 4.1.

The arithmetic cost of integers was studied by de Melo and Svaiter [dMS96], who obtained elementary universal bounds and lower bounds valid for almost all integers. Moreira [Mor97] sharpened the latter to the scale log⁡n/log⁡log​n\log n/\log\log n and established a matching asymptotic upper scale for all sufficiently large integers. These general estimates leave substantial room for special sequences: repeated squaring produces some very large integers with very short programs, and an almost-all lower bound does not determine the complexity of factorials or of their easiest multiples. Shub and Smale [SS95] showed that failure of a polynomial bound in log⁡k\log k for ultimate factorial complexity would imply Pℂ≠N​PℂP_{\mathbb{C}}\neq NP_{\mathbb{C}}. Upper bounds for μ⁡(k)\mu(k) thus form part of a broader study of explicit integers and algebraic complexity.

Further connections arise from the arithmetic complexity of explicit integer sequences. Koiran [Koi04] relates the construction of integers such as ⌊2n​log⁡2⌋\lfloor 2^{n}\log 2\rfloor to Valiant’s theory of arithmetic circuits. In particular, a polynomial-size constant-free circuit family for the permanent would give a polynomial bound in log⁡n\log n for the cost of this sequence. With the additional assumption P=P​S​P​A​C​EP=PSPACE, his results give such a bound for τ⁡(n!)\tau(n!) as well. Thus lower bounds for particular integer sequences can have consequences for polynomial circuit complexity, beyond the almost-all estimates for integers of a given size.

There is also a computational line of work on concrete upper bounds. Markström [Mar15] uses exhaustive searches for short straight-line programs to determine exact values and bounds for small factorials, primorials, and their ultimate complexities. These calculations complement asymptotic constructions by exhibiting short programs for individual integers. On the asymptotic side, successive multiplication gives μ⁡(k)≤τ⁡(k!)=O⁡(k)\mu(k)\leq\tau(k!)=O(k), while Strassen’s factorial algorithm gives the bound τ⁡(k!)=O⁡(k​(log⁡k)2)\tau(k!)=O(\sqrt{k}(\log k)^{2}); see [Mar15, Section 2]. The possibility of choosing a multiple of k!k! permits the much smaller bounds discussed next.

Cheng [Che04, Conjecture 1 and Theorem 1] obtained

μ⁡(k)≤exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡k​log⁡log​k))\mu(k)\leq\exp\!\left(O(\sqrt{\log k\log\log k})\right)

under a conjecture about smooth numbers in the elliptic Hasse intervals [p+1−2​p,p+1+2​p][p+1-2\sqrt{p},p+1+2\sqrt{p}]. Writing Lp​[a]=exp⁡(a​log⁡p​log⁡log​p)L_{p}[a]=\exp(a\sqrt{\log p\log\log p}), that conjecture asks, for every fixed a>0a>0, for pLp[−1/(2a)+o(1)]\sqrt{p}\,L_{p}[-1/(2a)+o(1)] many Lp​[a]L_{p}[a]-smooth integers in such an interval. His construction uses elliptic-curve division polynomials and also gives a randomized subexponential-time procedure for producing the programs.

The interval length in this conjecture is essential. Younis [You24, Theorem 1.3], assuming RH, proves smooth-number asymptotics for xθ≤h≤xx^{\theta}\leq h\leq x and (log⁡x)K⁡(θ)≤y≤2​x(\log x)^{K(\theta)}\leq y\leq 2x, for each fixed θ>1/2\theta>1/2. Cheng’s smoothness scale exceeds this lower bound on yy, but his intervals have length 4​p4\sqrt{p} at centers comparable to pp. For every fixed θ>1/2\theta>1/2, 4​p/pθ→04\sqrt{p}/p^{\theta}\to 0. Consequently, Younis’s RH theorem does not establish Cheng’s conjecture: the endpoint interval scale remains outside its stated range.

A different algebraic construction changes the required interval scale. Zhang [Zha26, Theorem 1.2] obtained the unconditional bound

μ⁡(k)≤exp⁡(O⁡((log⁡k)2/3​(log⁡log⁡k)1/3))\mu(k)\leq\exp\!\left(O((\log k)^{2/3}(\log\log k)^{1/3})\right)

using genus-two Jacobians, a family with a non-torsion marked divisor class, and integer circuits encoding nonzero arithmetic certificates. The order-counting theorem of Lenstra, Pila and Pomerance [LPP02, Theorem 1.1] supplies the relevant genus-two orders. The intervals used in this construction are

Ip=[p2−12​p3/2,p2+12​p3/2].I_{p}=\left[p^{2}-\frac{1}{2}p^{3/2},\,p^{2}+\frac{1}{2}p^{3/2}\right].

Their centers are of size p2p^{2} and their lengths are p3/2p^{3/2}, corresponding to the exponent 3/43/4 rather than 1/21/2.

The main contribution here is to recover Cheng’s square-root logarithmic upper-bound scale by combining this genus-two construction with a short-interval smooth-number estimate under a quasi-Riemann hypothesis. More precisely, any fixed δ>0\delta>0 with ζ⁡(s)≠0\zeta(s)\neq 0 for ℜ⁡(s)>1−δ\Re(s)>1-\delta, s≠1s\neq 1, suffices. Theorem B proves the required density estimate at every sufficiently large center on the x3/4x^{3/4} interval scale, with smoothness cutoff exp⁡(log⁡x​log⁡log​x)\exp(\sqrt{\log x\log\log x}). The transfer in Section 4 then yields the bound for μ⁡(k)\mu(k) with all integer gates charged. This removes the need for Cheng’s smooth-number conjecture in obtaining that upper-bound scale; it does not prove the conjecture itself. The genus-two family and certificate construction are those of [Zha26], while the analytic argument adapts Younis’s contour method to the fixed-strip hypothesis.

Our main result is the following.

Theorem A (Positive factorial multiples).

Assume that a fixed real number 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2 satisfies

ζ⁡(s)≠0(ℜ⁡(s)>1−δ,s≠1).\zeta(s)\neq 0\qquad\bigl(\Re(s)>1-\delta,\ s\neq 1\bigr).

There are constants C>0C>0 and k0≥3k_{0}\geq 3, depending only on δ\delta, such that, for every integer k≥k0k\geq k_{0}, there is a positive integer mkm_{k} satisfying

τ⁡(mk​k!)≤exp⁡(C​log⁡k​log⁡log​k).\tau(m_{k}k!)\leq\exp\!\left(C\sqrt{\log k\log\log k}\right).

All logarithms are natural. The constants may depend on δ\delta but are independent of kk.

The multiplier is a positive integer existence witness. The circuit computes the multiple mk​k!m_{k}k! from 11 and 22.

The new ingredient concerns smooth integers at every sufficiently large real center. We use the counting function Ψ⁡(x,y)\Psi(x,y) and saddle point α⁡(x,y)\alpha(x,y) defined in Definition 2.1.

Theorem B (Smooth integers under a fixed-strip hypothesis).

Assume that a fixed real number 0<δ≤1/20<\delta\leq 1/2 satisfies

ζ⁡(s)≠0(ℜ⁡(s)>1−δ,s≠1).\zeta(s)\neq 0\qquad\bigl(\Re(s)>1-\delta,\ s\neq 1\bigr).

For x>ex>e, put

L=log⁡x,S=L​log⁡L,y=eS,u=LS,L=\log x,\qquad S=\sqrt{L\log L},\qquad y=e^{S},\qquad u=\frac{L}{S},

and let α=α⁡(x,y)>0\alpha=\alpha(x,y)>0 be determined by

∑q≤yq​primelog⁡qqα−1=L.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq y\\ q\ {\rm prime}\end{subarray}}\frac{\log q}{q^{\alpha}-1}=L.

There are constants CδC_{\delta} and XδX_{\delta}, depending only on δ\delta, such that, for every real x≥Xδx\geq X_{\delta} and every real hh with x3/4≤h≤xx^{3/4}\leq h\leq x,

|Ψ⁡(x+h,y)−Ψ⁡(x,y)α⁡(h/x)​Ψ​(x,y)−1|≤Cδu.\left|\frac{\Psi(x+h,y)-\Psi(x,y)}{\alpha(h/x)\Psi(x,y)}-1\right|\leq\frac{C_{\delta}}{u}.

After increasing XδX_{\delta}, the same range satisfies

Ψ⁡(x+h,y)−Ψ⁡(x,y)≥h4​exp⁡(−3​log⁡x​log⁡log​x).\Psi(x+h,y)-\Psi(x,y)\geq\frac{h}{4}\exp\!\left(-3\sqrt{\log x\log\log x}\right).

The analytic method underlying Theorem B follows [You24, Section 3]. In particular, the construction of the contour as the right envelope of a central path, paths associated with zeta zeros, and a remaining vertical line is adapted from that work. Sections 2 and 3 supply the details needed to apply this method under the fixed hypothesis ζ⁡(s)≠0\zeta(s)\neq 0 for ℜ⁡(s)>1−δ\Re(s)>1-\delta, s≠1s\neq 1. Section 2 collects the unconditional estimates used in the argument, and Section 3 verifies the local shift, the envelope construction, and the contributions of all contour pieces for y=exp⁡(log⁡x​log⁡log​x)y=\exp(\sqrt{\log x\log\log x}) and x3/4≤h≤xx^{3/4}\leq h\leq x. These verifications yield thresholds depending on δ\delta and estimates uniform in hh; the underlying contour construction is due to Younis.

The factor α\alpha is retained throughout, including at h=xh=x. Recent AI-assisted work addresses the fixed-half-plane hypothesis directly in the classical setting. OpenAI’s preprints [OA26a, OA26b] report proofs of nonvanishing for ℜ⁡(s)>7/8\Re(s)>7/8 and ℜ⁡(s)>11/12\Re(s)>11/12, respectively; the latter is a shorter argument written with human assistance. These conclusions supply the hypothesis of Theorems A and B with δ=1/8\delta=1/8 and δ=1/12\delta=1/12, respectively. Cureton and Thorner [CT26, Theorem 1.1] report the corresponding result for Dedekind zeta functions over arbitrary number fields, with δ=1/6000\delta=1/6000. For our application, the classical Riemann zeta function alone is sufficient. We state both theorems with their common zero-free hypothesis explicit and prove the resulting implications below; either of the reported classical nonvanishing results then yields an unconditional specialization. In that specialization, the deduction of the square-root logarithmic bound is complete using the cited arithmetic inputs and Theorem B; no separate conjecture about smooth numbers in elliptic Hasse intervals is required.

The local shift uses [You24, Lemma 2.3], with the fixed positive strip width making its errors small at the chosen value of yy. Zero density bounds the sum of the retained zero paths. The other analytic inputs are the unconditional estimates in [You24, (1.3), (1.5), (1.6), (1.9), (1.13), and Lemma 3.6].

The arithmetic construction is inherited from [Zha26]. Its marked family is given by [Zha26, (7)–(9) and Lemma 4.1]. We use its charged positive certificate [Zha26, Proposition 5.1] and its transfer to the marked slice [Zha26, Lemma 6.1]. Recording rational failures and amplifying prime support are the constructions of [Zha26, Lemmas 3.2 and 3.1]. These are established ingredients of the present proof.

Section 2 fixes the analytic notation and records the exact unconditional inputs. Section 3 proves Theorem B, including the local shift, central curves and horizontal connectors. Section 4 gives the density-to-complexity transfer with all gate costs and proves Theorem A.

2. Preliminaries

We use the smooth-number notation and saddle-point estimates of [You24], with natural logarithms and real interval endpoints.

The von Mangoldt function is

Λ⁡(n)={log⁡q,n=qj,q​ prime,j≥1,0,otherwise.\Lambda(n)=\begin{cases}\log q,&n=q^{j},\quad q\text{ prime},\quad j\geq 1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
Definition 2.1 (Smooth integers and the saddle point).

A positive integer is yy-smooth if all its prime divisors are at most yy; the integer 11 is included. For real x≥y≥2x\geq y\geq 2, define

Ψ(x,y)=#{n∈ℕ∣n≤x,n is y-smooth},Zy(s)=∏q≤yq​prime(1−q−s)−1(ℜ(s)>0).\Psi(x,y)=\#\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid n\leq x,\ n\text{ is }y\text{-smooth}\},\qquad Z_{y}(s)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq y\\ q\ {\rm prime}\end{subarray}}(1-q^{-s})^{-1}\quad(\Re(s)>0).

Let α=α⁡(x,y)>0\alpha=\alpha(x,y)>0 be the unique solution of

Fy​(α)=log⁡x,Fy​(a)=∑q≤yq​primelog⁡qqa−1.F_{y}(\alpha)=\log x,\qquad F_{y}(a)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq y\\ q\ {\rm prime}\end{subarray}}\frac{\log q}{q^{a}-1}.

Equivalently, α\alpha uniquely minimizes xa​Zy​(a)x^{a}Z_{y}(a) over a>0a>0.

The function FyF_{y} is continuous and strictly decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Its limits at the two endpoints are ∞\infty and 00, respectively. This proves existence and uniqueness in Definition 2.1. The equivalence follows from

dd​a​log⁡(xa​Zy​(a))=log⁡x−Fy​(a).\frac{d}{da}\log(x^{a}Z_{y}(a))=\log x-F_{y}(a).

For ℜ⁡(s)>0\Re(s)>0, each Euler factor is holomorphic and nonzero, since |q−s|<1|q^{-s}|<1. Differentiating the finite product and expanding a geometric series gives

(2.1) −Zy′​(s)Zy​(s)=∑q≤ylog⁡qqs−1=∑q≤y∑j≥1(log⁡q)​q−j​s.-\frac{Z_{y}^{\prime}(s)}{Z_{y}(s)}=\sum_{q\leq y}\frac{\log q}{q^{s}-1}=\sum_{q\leq y}\sum_{j\geq 1}(\log q)q^{-js}.

On the other hand,

∑n≤yΛ⁡(n)​n−s=∑q​prime,j≥1qj≤y(log⁡q)​q−j​s.\sum_{n\leq y}\Lambda(n)n^{-s}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\ {\rm prime},\ j\geq 1\\ q^{j}\leq y\end{subarray}}(\log q)q^{-js}.

Consequently,

(2.2) −Zy′​(s)Zy​(s)=∑n≤yΛ⁡(n)​n−s+Ry​(s),Ry​(s):=∑q≤y,j≥2qj>y(log⁡q)​q−j​s,-\frac{Z_{y}^{\prime}(s)}{Z_{y}(s)}=\sum_{n\leq y}\Lambda(n)n^{-s}+R_{y}(s),\qquad R_{y}(s):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq y,\ j\geq 2\\ q^{j}>y\end{subarray}}(\log q)q^{-js},

where qq ranges over primes. Only exponents j≥2j\geq 2 occur in the remainder, because q≤yq\leq y.

3. Fixed-strip short intervals

In this section, we prove Theorem B by establishing the local shift and then estimating every part of the counting contour.

3.1. A long-interval estimate

Proposition 3.1 (Long-interval density and a saddle-point lower bound).

For all real x≥y≥16x\geq y\geq 16,

(3.1) Ψ⁡(x,y)≥x​exp⁡(−log⁡y−log⁡xlog⁡y​log⁡(8​log⁡x)).\Psi(x,y)\geq x\exp\!\left(-\log y-\frac{\log x}{\log y}\log(8\log x)\right).

There is an absolute x0>ex_{0}>e such that, for every real x≥x0x\geq x_{0}, writing

L=log⁡x,S=L​log⁡L,y=eS,L=\log x,\qquad S=\sqrt{L\log L},\qquad y=e^{S},

we have

(3.2) Ψ⁡(x,y)≥x​e−3​S\Psi(x,y)\geq xe^{-3S}

and

(3.3) α⁡(x,y)≥1−2​log⁡LS>12.\alpha(x,y)\geq 1-\frac{2\log L}{S}>\frac{1}{2}.
Proof.

We first obtain the prime-counting estimate needed for the argument. Let π⁡(t)\pi(t) count primes at most tt, and take t≥16t\geq 16. Put n=⌊t/2⌋n=\lfloor t/2\rfloor. Then n≥8n\geq 8 and n≥t/4n\geq t/4. Since the central binomial coefficient is the largest coefficient of order 2​n2n,

(2​nn)≥4n2​n+1≥2n.\binom{2n}{n}\geq\frac{4^{n}}{2n+1}\geq 2^{n}.

Here 2​n+1≤2n2n+1\leq 2^{n} for n≥3n\geq 3, as follows by induction. For each prime qq, let vq​(N)v_{q}(N) denote the exponent of qq in the prime factorization of NN. Then

vq​(2​nn)=∑j≥1(⌊2​nqj⌋−2​⌊nqj⌋).v_{q}\!\binom{2n}{n}=\sum_{j\geq 1}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{q^{j}}\right\rfloor-2\left\lfloor\frac{n}{q^{j}}\right\rfloor\right).

Each summand is either zero or one, and it vanishes when qj>2​nq^{j}>2n. Thus qvq​((2​nn))≤2​nq^{v_{q}(\binom{2n}{n})}\leq 2n for every prime q≤2​nq\leq 2n, and

2n≤(2​nn)≤(2​n)π⁡(2​n)≤tπ⁡(t).2^{n}\leq\binom{2n}{n}\leq(2n)^{\pi(2n)}\leq t^{\pi(t)}.

Taking logarithms gives

(3.4) π⁡(t)≥n​log⁡2log⁡t≥t​log⁡24​log⁡t≥t8​log⁡t.\pi(t)\geq\frac{n\log 2}{\log t}\geq\frac{t\log 2}{4\log t}\geq\frac{t}{8\log t}.

Now let x≥y≥16x\geq y\geq 16, and put

4. Arithmetic transfer and the final bound

In this section, we transfer the density conclusion of Theorem B to actual integer circuits, using the established certificate and marked-slice transfer of [Zha26].

We follow the straight-line program convention of de Melo and Svaiter [dMS96] and the notation of [Zha26, Definition 1.1].

Definition 4.1 (Arithmetic complexity).

An integer straight-line program begins with 11 and 22; each subsequent gate adds, subtracts or multiplies two available values. Values computed earlier may be reused. The length is the number of gates, independent of the bit lengths of their operands. For n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, let τ⁡(n)\tau(n) denote the minimum length of such a program producing nn. For an integer k≥2k\geq 2, define

μ⁡(k)=minm∈ℤ>0⁡τ⁡(m​k!).\mu(k)=\min_{m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}}\tau(mk!).

Only these three binary operations are counted as gates. Other integer constants must be constructed, and division, modular reduction, gcd, determinant and group operations must be implemented by the allowed operations whenever they are used in a circuit. Starting from 11 alone changes τ\tau by at most one operation. Allowing negative nonzero multipliers in the definition of μ\mu changes the minimum by at most a constant, since the sign can be reversed using a bounded number of arithmetic operations.

4.1. The cited family and arithmetic inputs

Definition 4.2 (The marked quintic family).

For integers H≥1H\geq 1 and 𝐳=(z1,…,z5)∈{0,…,H−1}5\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{5})\in\{0,\ldots,H-1\}^{5}, put

(4.1) t1\displaystyle t_{1} =1+3z1,ti=3zi(2≤i≤5),\displaystyle=1+3z_{1},\qquad t_{i}=3z_{i}\quad(2\leq i\leq 5),
(4.2) f𝐳​(X)\displaystyle f_{\mathbf{z}}(X) =(1+310​t5)​X5+∑i=1432​i​ti​Xi−∑i=15ti.\displaystyle=(1+3^{10}t_{5})X^{5}+\sum_{i=1}^{4}3^{2i}t_{i}X^{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{5}t_{i}.

Let C𝐳C_{\mathbf{z}} be the smooth completion of Y2=f𝐳​(X)Y^{2}=f_{\mathbf{z}}(X), and set

P𝐳=(1/9,1/243),D𝐳=[P𝐳−∞].P_{\mathbf{z}}=(1/9,1/243),\qquad D_{\mathbf{z}}=[P_{\mathbf{z}}-\infty].

These are the family and marked class of [Zha26, (7)–(9)]. The same polynomial formulas define the family for 𝐳∈𝔽p5\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{5}. For a prime p≥3p\geq 3, write

xp=p2−12​p3/2,Ip=[xp,xp+p3/2],Sp=log⁡xp​log⁡log⁡xp.x_{p}=p^{2}-\frac{1}{2}p^{3/2},\qquad I_{p}=[x_{p},x_{p}+p^{3/2}],\qquad S_{p}=\sqrt{\log x_{p}\log\log x_{p}}.

For the permitted integer vectors, smoothness, good reduction at 33 and infinite order of D𝐳D_{\mathbf{z}} are proved in [Zha26, Lemma 4.1]. We use the following two consequences as cited results.

Proposition 4.3 (Charged positive certificates, [Zha26, Proposition 5.1]).

There is an absolute constant C0≥1C_{0}\geq 1 such that, for every pair of integers N,H≥1N,H\geq 1 and every permitted vector 𝐳\mathbf{z}, there is a positive integer Z⁡(N,𝐳)Z(N,\mathbf{z}) with

τ⁡(Z⁡(N,𝐳))≤C0​(1+⌈log2⁡N⌉+⌈log2⁡(H+1)⌉).\tau(Z(N,\mathbf{z}))\leq C_{0}\left(1+\lceil\log_{2}N\rceil+\lceil\log_{2}(H+1)\rceil\right).

Its circuit is fixed from the rational data N,𝐳N,\mathbf{z}, independently of a tested prime. Its output is divisible by 22 and 33. For every prime p≥5p\geq 5, its output is divisible by pp if either

  1. (1)

    f𝐳f_{\mathbf{z}} modulo pp fails to be a squarefree quintic; or

  2. (2)

    f𝐳f_{\mathbf{z}} modulo pp is a squarefree quintic and [N]​(D𝐳modp)=0[N](D_{\mathbf{z}}\bmod p)=0 in Jac⁡(C𝐳modp)​(𝔽p)\Jac(C_{\mathbf{z}}\bmod p)(\mathbb{F}_{p}).

The bound is for circuits in Definition 4.1.

The charge in Proposition 4.3 includes all five literal coordinates, scalar scheduling, bounded-degree coefficient arithmetic, and every retained inverse of a rationally nonzero branch test. Complete divisor arithmetic is expanded into scalar instructions in [Zha26, Proposition 5.1]; rational failures are then recorded by [Zha26, Lemma 3.2], and the nonzero integer output is squared. The scalar schedule uses at most 2​⌊log2⁡N⌋2\lfloor\log_{2}N\rfloor group additions before that expansion. These statements supply no free scalar register, division, gcd, determinant, zero-test or group-operation gate.

The algebraic references behind the cited construction are complete composition, reduction and unique reduced representatives in [Gal12, Theorems 10.3.14, 10.3.21 and 10.4.1], the general reduction algorithm in [KS06, Section 2, Algorithm 1], and compatibility of relative Jacobians with good reduction in [Mil21, Section 8, Theorem 8.1, and the proof of Corollary 12.3]. Only the general reduction algorithm from [KS06] is relevant; its special endomorphism families are not used.

Proposition 4.4 (The full marked-slice probability, [Zha26, Lemma 6.1]).

Let p>8100p>8100 be prime and let 𝒜⊆Ip∩ℤ\mathcal{A}\subseteq I_{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}. For uniform 𝐳∈𝔽p5\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{5}, with f𝐳f_{\mathbf{z}} given by (4.1)–(4.2),

Pr⁡(f𝐳​ is a squarefree quintic,#​Jac⁡(C𝐳)​(𝔽p)∈𝒜)≥max⁡(|𝒜|−p,0)48000​p3/2​(log⁡p)2​(log⁡log⁡p)2.\Pr\!\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{\mathbf{z}}\text{ is a squarefree quintic},\\ \#\Jac(C_{\mathbf{z}})(\mathbb{F}_{p})\in\mathcal{A}\end{array}\right)\geq\frac{\max(|\mathcal{A}|-p,0)}{48000p^{3/2}(\log p)^{2}(\log\log p)^{2}}.

Proposition 4.4 transfers the full quintic model count of [LPP02, Theorem 1.1, p. 106]. That theorem allows arbitrary nonzero leading coefficients and at most pp exceptional integer orders. The transfer in [Zha26, Lemma 6.1] uses a bijection of triples to pass to the marked slice. It does not restrict the original count to monic quintics. We use this probability statement directly.
